The last part ended with a line that answered our question well in one stretch of the time course, badly in another, and not at all in a third, and with a promise: the next part keeps the question and changes what we mean by noise. Here is what that means at the bench. A tissue area is a continuous quantity, and a bell curve around a straight line is a decent description of how it scatters. Now walk to the next bench. A mouse either crosses the wire or it doesn't. A tissue section holds some number of PDGFR-β+ cells, a whole number that cannot go below zero. A mouse spends some share of a five-minute open-field session in the center of the arena, a number stuck between zero and one. A crossing time cannot be negative either, and it comes with the occasional extreme value. None of these scatter the way a bell curve says they should, and a line fitted to them will happily predict half a mouse, minus three cells, or 110% of the time on the wire.

This part keeps everything you already know and changes one thing. The recipe has three ingredients, and it is the same recipe in every chapter: pick a family, which says how the outcome scatters; keep the linear predictor you already know how to write; and choose a link, the doorway between the two. This opening page has two jobs. It explains what changes when we leave the Gaussian world, and why we have to. And it is the map of the part, which you will find at the end. It fits nothing: the models belong to the chapters that follow.

![Pick a family, keep the linear predictor, choose the link. One plug, a few adapters, and a socket for every kind of outcome.](images/linear-models-intro_one-plug-many-adapters.png){#fig-glm-intro-adapter fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a wooden table with an electrical cord ending in a plug with a teal head, two loose adapter heads in ochre and blush-grey beside it, and three differently shaped wall sockets in teal, ochre and blush-grey on the wall behind."}

## Cells are counted, not measured {#sec-glm-intro}

If you have ever counted cells under a microscope, you have already measured an outcome that lives in a smaller world than the whole number line. `cell_data` has a column we haven't touched, `Pdgfrb_Pos`, the number of PDGFR-β-positive cells counted in each animal's tissue section, and it will be our example for the whole page. I'm not going to model it yet. I only want you to look at it, because everything in this part starts from looking.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(cell_data, aes(x = DPI_f, y = Pdgfrb_Pos)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = Condition, shape = Condition),
              width = 0.12, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5,
               linewidth = 0.4, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(SHAM = "#D55E00", MCAO = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "PDGFR-β+ cells per section") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![PDGFR-$\beta$-positive cell counts per animal, by day after ischemia (day 0 is the sham group)](glm-intro_files/figure-html/fig-glm_counts_by_dpi-1.png){#fig-glm_counts_by_dpi width=624}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sd_day <- tapply(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos, cell_data$DPI_f, sd)
```
:::






Two things jump out, and I'd like you to notice them before I name them. On days 0 and 3 the counts sit low, around 500, in a fairly tight cluster pressed against the floor of the plot. From day 7 they climb to two or three thousand and *fan out*: the standard deviation of the counts goes from about 190 cells on day 0 to about 920 at the widest. The floor is a zero you can't go below. The fan is a spread that grows with the mean. A count has both of those properties, always.

### What a linear model quietly assumed

In the last part, every model said the same two things about an observation, whether we wrote them down or not. The first was that the outcome can be *any* real number: the line gives a mean, and a bell curve around it allows values above and below, positive and negative, whole or fractional. The second was that the width of the bell is the same everywhere: one `sigma` for the whole dataset. @sec-linear-regression-multiple ended on exactly how uncomfortable that second promise can get.

A count breaks both. It cannot be negative, and it cannot be 412.7, so a bell curve spends part of its mass on values the world doesn't contain. And its spread is not constant, because a section with two thousand cells has more room to differ from its neighbors than one with five hundred. Notice what has *not* gone wrong: the line. A straight line through the day means was a perfectly respectable description of where the counts sit. What fails is the assumption about the noise around it, and that is why no amount of care in `lm()` rescues you. You can transform, trim and rescale, but you are still asking a bell curve to describe something that isn't bell-shaped. We'll watch it fail on these very counts, with a fitted model and its predictions, in @sec-count-regression. Here I only want to name the cause.

The same diagnosis covers the other outcomes of this part, each broken in its own way. A yes or a no can only be 0 or 1, and how much it varies depends on how likely the yes is. A proportion is trapped between 0 and 1. A crossing time is positive, skewed to the right, and sprinkled with the occasional extreme value. None of them is "a continuous measurement with some noise", and pretending otherwise is a choice with a cost.

## What a GLM actually is

Here's the way I like to think about the fix. Suppose you do your arithmetic in a room with no walls: any number, positive or negative, is fine, and adding one thing to another always makes sense. That's where the linear predictor lives, the part you already know: $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots$. Now suppose the quantity you actually care about (the expected count) lives in a smaller room, one that only admits valid values. You need a doorway between the two rooms: something that takes whatever number the linear predictor produces and translates it into a value the small room accepts. And you need to say what kind of noise the outcome has once you're in the small room, because a count is noisy in a different way than a tissue area. A generalized linear model is exactly those three choices, made explicitly [@mcelreath2020; @inchausti2023]:

1. [A family]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: the probability distribution that describes the scatter of the outcome around its mean. (Gaussian, Poisson, binomial, and others.)
2. [A linear predictor]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} $\eta_i$: the additive combination of predictors you already know how to write.
3. [A link function]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} $g$: the doorway. It connects the mean of the outcome, $\mu_i$, to the linear predictor.

$$
y_i \sim \text{Family}(\mu_i, \dots), \qquad g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_k x_{ki}
$$ {#eq-glm}

Read the second half in both directions. The link $g$ takes the mean to the unbounded scale; its inverse $g^{-1}$ takes the linear predictor back to a valid mean, $\mu_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i)$. Software does the second one whenever it predicts.

![The linear predictor lives in a room with no walls, where any number is welcome. The mean you care about lives in a smaller room. The link is the doorway between them.](images/glm-intro_two-rooms-one-doorway.png){#fig-glm-intro-rooms fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor cutaway of two adjoining spaces: a wall-less pale-teal expanse on the left with colored pebbles scattered widely toward the horizon, and a small tidy room on the right with a row of pebbles on its floor, joined by an open wooden door with a dotted arc carrying one pebble through it."}

That's a lot of new vocabulary for something you've been doing since @sec-linear-regression-what. The reassuring part: **everything you've fit so far is already a GLM.** A Gaussian family with the *identity* link ($g(\mu) = \mu$, the doorway that changes nothing) is @eq-linear-regression-simple, with no new machinery at all. The reason we never needed a doorway is that a Gaussian mean is allowed to be any real number, so the unbounded room and the small room were the same room. Counts and proportions aren't so lucky. Here is what the doorways look like.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
eta <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 200)

links <- rbind(
  data.frame(eta = eta, mu = eta, link = "Identity"),
  data.frame(eta = eta, mu = exp(eta), link = "Log (inverse: exp)"),
  data.frame(eta = eta, mu = plogis(eta), link = "Logit (inverse: logistic)")
)
links$link <- factor(links$link, levels = unique(links$link))

ggplot(links, aes(x = eta, y = mu)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~link, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Linear predictor (η)", y = "Mean on the outcome scale (μ)") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Three inverse links, each translating an unbounded linear predictor into a valid mean](glm-intro_files/figure-html/fig-glm_links-1.png){#fig-glm_links width=672}
:::
:::






I drew the dashed zero line in every panel on purpose. In the first panel, the line crosses it: a Gaussian model with an identity link will cheerfully predict negative values if the linear predictor goes there. In the second, the exponential curve approaches zero forever and never crosses it, so no matter how negative $\eta$ gets, $\mu = e^{\eta}$ stays positive. That's the doorway for counts. In the third, the logistic curve squeezes the whole real line into the interval between 0 and 1, which is the doorway for proportions and for yes/no outcomes. The families and links this book will use, and where they show up, are collected below. Keep it open next to the data you actually have.

| If your outcome is... | Family | Link | Where |
|:-------------------------|:-------------------|:------------|:------------------------|
| A continuous measurement (tissue area) | Gaussian | Identity | @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous, @sec-linear-regression-multiple |
| A count of cells or spikes | Poisson, negative binomial | Log | @sec-count-regression |
| A yes or a no | Bernoulli | Logit | @sec-logistic-regression |
| Successes out of a known number of trials | Binomial, beta-binomial | Logit | @sec-logistic-regression, @sec-beta-robust-regression |
| A proportion strictly between 0 and 1 | Beta | Logit | @sec-beta-robust-regression |
| A positive, skewed value with the odd extreme one (crossing time) | Student-t | Identity, on the log scale | @sec-beta-robust-regression |
| Ordered categories (a deficit score) | Cumulative | Logit | Ordinal regression, later in the book |

: The families and links this book uses, and where each appears. {#tbl-glm_families}

::: callout-tip
### Don't pick the family by staring at a histogram

It's tempting to look at the shape of the outcome's histogram and choose a family to match. McElreath's name for this is "histomancy", and his objection is that it's the wrong evidence [@mcelreath2020]. What decides the family is what the outcome *is*: a number of cells is a whole number that can't go below zero; a number of successes out of a known number of trials can't exceed the trials. Those facts constrain the family before you've looked at a single value. The histogram of the raw outcome also pools animals from different conditions, so it can look lumpy or smooth for reasons that have nothing to do with the family.
:::

## What changes when you read the result

The doorway has a price, and it is worth knowing before you meet the first coefficient. Coefficients now live on the *link* scale, not on the scale of the outcome you measured. With a log link, adding a number on the link scale means *multiplying* on the outcome scale: a coefficient of 0.7 does not add 0.7 cells, it multiplies the expected count by $e^{0.7}$, about 2. It is the same kind of arithmetic as pH, where each unit is a factor of ten rather than a fixed amount, and it is usually the honest way to describe how cell counts change anyway ("twice as many", not "a thousand more"). With a logit link the coefficient is a change in log-odds, a scale that deserves its own chapter and gets one in @sec-logistic-regression. Either way, you read a coefficient by translating it back through the inverse link, which is exactly what the software does when it predicts.

![On the log scale you add a step, and on the count scale you multiply. Each stair roughly doubles the pile.](images/glm-intro_each-step-doubles.png){#fig-glm-intro-steps fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a wooden staircase of five steps climbing from left to right, with towers of teal and ochre petri dishes growing from a single dish on the first step to a tall stack on the last, and small teal arrows curving from each step to the next."}

::: callout-warning
### A word about priors on the link scale

A habit from Gaussian models can hurt you here. On the log scale, a prior that looks timid, like a Normal with a standard deviation of 10 on a coefficient, is not vague on the count scale: it says a change of 20 log-units is plausible, which is a factor of hundreds of millions. Priors on link-scale coefficients need to be judged by what they imply on the *outcome* scale, which @sec-priors-regularization taught you to do with a prior predictive check.
:::

## What stays the same

Less changes than the vocabulary suggests. The workflow of the first part is untouched: you state a question, fit a model, ask whether the model could have produced data like yours with a posterior predictive check (see @sec-mcmc-model-checking), and improve it. Every applied model is still fitted with `brms` and with its frequentist counterpart, `glm()` or a close relative, side by side. The linear predictor is exactly the one you have been writing since @sec-linear-regression-what, with categorical predictors, interactions and centering all working as before. And the family is not a ritual: it is a statement about the noise, so it is something you check, not something you pick and forget.

That last point is the quiet link back to the last part. There, a single `sigma` was too stingy for one day and too generous for others, and the fix I pointed to was to model `sigma` itself as a function of the predictor. A GLM's family already does a version of that, automatically, because it ties the variance to the mean. Choosing a family is choosing a model for the variance, and in the chapters ahead it will be the variance, not the mean, that breaks first. A regression is not only a model for where the middle of the data sits; it can be a model for how the whole distribution behaves, and the GLM is the first place where that becomes visible. <!-- TODO: link @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression, where sigma itself depends on predictors, once that chapter exists. -->

## What you'll do in the next three chapters

**First we estimate how likely a mouse is to cross the wire** (@sec-logistic-regression). In the hanging wire test a mouse completes its crossings or it doesn't: a single yes or no is the coarsest measurement in science and the one we meet most often. We take the logit link on its own terms, learn to say what a genotype did to the *chance* of completing the test in a sentence a reviewer can use, three different ways, and check that the model behind the sentence is not fooling us. We also see what happens when many yes/no answers are pooled into successes out of a number of trials, using the proportion of PDGFR-β+ cells from the data above.

**Next we count cells and spikes** (@sec-count-regression). This is where the counts on this page finally get a model: we watch a Gaussian fail on them, swap the family for a Poisson and then a negative binomial, and read the result as a ratio. Then the counts get what they were missing, a denominator (a count of cells means little until you know how much tissue it came from, and a count of spikes means little until you know how long you listened). Then we meet a pile of zeros in real human neurons and ask whether it is what it looks like.

**And we close by measuring behavior** (@sec-beta-robust-regression). Each mouse made nine attempts on the wire, so the single yes or no of the first chapter becomes successes out of nine, and a plain binomial turns out to be too sure of itself. Then come crossing times with the occasional extreme value and, on a different bench, a proportion that is the measurement itself (the share of a five-minute open-field session that a mouse spends in the center, and what a stroke does to it). Three outcomes, three small changes to the recipe, and a closing look at what this whole part has quietly assumed, which is where the next part picks up.

## Three things to know before you start

First, **the data keep growing**. This page stayed with the histology data, `cell_data`, the same ones that carried the last part. The hanging wire test, the open field and the spikes come with their own datasets, each introduced in the first chapter that uses it, with a plain account of what one row is and how it was obtained. That habit matters more as the outcomes get less familiar: before you trust a model for a spike count, you should know what was counted.

Second, **the two lenses stay on**. Every applied model is fitted with `brms` and with its frequentist counterpart, in tabs, and each chapter closes by saying where the two agree and where they part ways. One practical note you will meet more than once: `parsnip` has no engine for some of the families in this part (beta regression, beta-binomial, Student-t), so there the frequentist side is `glmmTMB`, and the chapter says so rather than quietly dropping the comparison.

Third, **one thing is deliberately left for later**. Throughout this part, every row is treated as an independent observation: one row per animal in the histology data, one row per mouse in the wire data, one row per neuron and trial in the spike data. Where a chapter touches data that really are nested (several attempts inside a mouse, or several trials inside a neuron, for instance) it treats the attempts as independent *on purpose*, and it tells you what that costs. Those are the cracks that the hierarchical models of the next part are built to seal. I'd rather you meet the problem once you can recognize it than have me hide it.

So let's start with the simplest outcome there is. On to @sec-logistic-regression.
